Fifty-eight comments

Words

I’m fairly sure I’ve heard words that go with this tune. I don’t remember the words except that every second bar was “Paddy O‘Rafferty” so it went “Something something Paddy O’ Rafferty, something something Paddy O’ Rafferty”.

If you can associate that phrase that appears every four bars with the words “Paddy O’Rafferty”, I find it easier to remember the tune.

I’ve mentioned this before in connection to other tunes like “Geese in the bog” and “Merryily kissed the quaker” - having words really helps in remembering a melody. And it works the other way around of course, as any composer of radio jingles will tell you.

I wouldn’t call this “a damned good version” of “Paddy O’Rafferty” at all. It seems rather to be a conflation of the more or less standard versions of both “P O R” and “Ten (aka Six) Penny Money”. Sticking two common tunes together to create a bigger tune does not constitute a version in any meaningful sense of the word.

↳ Posted by Dr. Dow on June 25th, 2007.

Paidin in A

Somebody mentioned this version of “Paidin O‘Rafferty” about 2 weeks ago. It’s the 5-part version in the key of A major recorded by “Patrick Street”, and subsequently Kevin Burke & Ged Foley. Deserves to be included as a tune in its’ own right, as it’s very different from the more common version in D with only 3 parts.

↳ Posted by Kenny on December 28th, 2007.

Well, this has survived so far, I’m glad to say. I had contributed a multi-part, a few more parts than this, with links to all the relatives, and history, and it was axed. Yeah, I’m still a bit sore about it. This also comes from that same root, and there are a few other in the family. My fingers are crossed for you Kenny. Let’s hope this remains, whatever the ‘associations’ that might pre-exist… ;-)

The pairing made use of similarities between the two tunes and created a natural harmony, a bit like what Luka Bloom would achieve weaving The Kesh jig into his chorus You couldn’t have come at a better time.

↳ Posted by NylonFlute on February 16th, 2022.

Paddy O’Rafferty, X:16

Version set by Beethoven in his 20 Irish Songs (WoO 153, no. 14), collected and edited by George Thomson.

The title for once is also “Paddy O‘Rafferty,” rather than some new title devised by Thomson and his poets, and the lyrics are in fact about Paddy O’Rafferty.

Lyrics by Sir Alexander Boswell (1775 - 1822):

Paddy O’Rafferty, merry and vigorous,
Laugh’d at his lot, tho‘ ’twas somewhat too rigorous;
Poor was his prize from the wheel of life’s lottery,
Turning the wheel in old Dennis Keogh’s pottery.
Still he kept turning, and still the clay tapering,
Grew a black pot to hold ink for with paper in,
Sometimes a brown jar to hoard a small pension in,
Sometimes, faith, something not worth a word’s mentioning.

Arrah, quoth Paddy, and so goes the round about,
So come those fortunes they make such a sound about,
Some in their save-alls their thousands are gathering,
Some from these ink-pots great families fathering.
So Mister Keogh I no longer will stay with ye,
Luck, whispers Paddy, take heart and away with ye,
Stout are your limbs, a good countenance carrying,
Why should not Paddy catch money by marrying?

Pat took the hint and gambol’d like a mountebank,
Small were his dealings with town or with county bank,
Short his accounts were, and no need of docqueting,
Light was his money-bag, easy in pocketing.
Up with his bundle, his trusty stick shouldering,
Set them, quoth Pat, stay at home and be mouldering;
But a smooth shilling I’d willingly now wager,
Paddy O’Rafferty hooks an old dowager.

Re: Paddy O’Rafferty

The lyrics here strongly suggest both having a chorus and that at least in Connemara it was one of many songs with parts, to delay closing time in the bar, that the various 5-part or 8-part versions in The Session are following from the remembered lyrics. With enough drink to help the memories around the bar, they’d be able to sing all night. Páidín sings parts, and his lady admirer sings parts, mentioning her weak hamstrings (’ioscaidí) and has to stand up and gallivant around him, perhaps a jig, as her bottom isn’t a part of a 3-legged wooden stool, in my understanding of the words. And being unacceptable to many ears over centuries, other parts of such a fine song get lost.

It’s also a ‘portaireacht’ or lilting tune elsewhere in Ireland.

https://songsinirish.com/paidin-o-raifeartaigh-lyrics/

Páidín Ó Raifeartaigh (5 Pts In A)

I went looking for this version of Páidín Ó Raifeartaigh on The Session, but unless it doesn’t include this spelling of the title, or it’s in another key, I didn’t find it, which was surprising. I don’t think it’s uncommon. If this is a duplicate, please be kind and add it where it belongs!

I don’t know where I first encountered it, perhaps my friend Daron Tansley, who plays several PÓ‘Rs beautifully on the whistle. This here is a basic setting based on Danny O’Mahony’s playing on his wonderful solo recording, In Retrospect. The tune listing for that track is (incorrectly) linked to a different version of the tune, which I hope to rectify now that the correct one is here to link to it (as soon as I figure out how!).
